1:
Henry gives Jethro two errands, and Wesley the same two after him. He came first to congratulate the happiness of Israel and the honour of Moses his son-in-law, having heard what all the country rang of; and now, Henry says, Jethro thinks himself well paid for all the kindness he had shown Moses in his distress. Though as a Midianite he was not to share with them in the promised land, he shared in the joy of their deliverance — and we may thus make the comforts of others our own, by taking pleasure, as God does, in the prosperity of the righteous. His second errand was to bring Moses's wife and children back to him. Henry defends the earlier separation, since Moses foresaw what discouragements he was likely to meet in the court of Pharaoh; but he insists that the parting could only be temporary, husbands being commanded to dwell with their wives, and observes that Jethro would not keep his daughter from her husband. Gill adds that the Targums style Jethro the prince of Midian, and Keil that Moses received his father-in-law with the honour due to his rank.

Whether Moses had in fact sent his family away is the question, and Calvin dissents from everyone. The greater number of commentators, he grants, think that Zipporah, enraged over her son's circumcision, turned back on the journey and went to live with her father; Clarke states that view, and allows the alternative that Moses sent them back, foreseeing the troubles they would meet in Egypt. To Calvin neither seems probable, and he gives three reasons. Moses would never have allowed his sons to be deprived of the redemption of which he was himself the minister; it would not have been consistent that they should afterwards be appointed priests, of whom God was not the Redeemer; and had he deposited his wife and children in safety and advanced alone to the contest, he would have been deservedly suspected of deceit, or of excessive cowardice. He has no doubt, therefore, that Moses underwent the yoke of bondage together with his household, and by that proof evidenced his faithfulness. The clause about sending her back he applies not to Egypt but to the wilderness, Moses having sent his wife to visit her father out of respect to an old man nearly connected with him.

The names of the two sons are read for their sense. Henry takes Gershom, a stranger, as designed for both a memorial of Moses's own condition and a memorandum to his son of his, since we are all strangers upon earth, as all our fathers were; and Eliezer, my God a help, he reads either backward to the deliverance from Pharaoh after the slaying of the Egyptian, or — if this was the son circumcised at the inn — forward, as the original will bear, the Lord is my help and will deliver me from the sword of Pharaoh. When we undertake any difficult service for God and our generation, he concludes, it is good to encourage ourselves in God as our help, since he that has delivered does and will deliver. Calvin finds in the same names a proof of magnanimity: Moses cannot but have brought on himself the ill-will of his connections by calling their country a strange land. Ellicott follows Eliezer further, supposing him the boy Zipporah circumcised in the wilderness, who grew to manhood and had a son Rehabiah whose descendants were very numerous in the time of David; whether Moses named him before parting from him, in allusion to his escape from the Pharaoh who sought to slay him, or first on receiving him back, in allusion to the host destroyed in the sea, Ellicott leaves uncertain. Henry adds a chronological caution: the incident may well have happened where it stands, before the giving of the law.
5:
Clarke thinks the whole visit is out of its chronological place, and lays out his reasons at length. Jethro is said to come while Israel is encamped at the mount of God, yet by the following chapter they had not yet reached Horeb and did not arrive there till the third month after leaving Egypt, whereas the transactions this account is joined to fall in the second. Moses himself, in the opening of Deuteronomy, relates that it was when they were about to depart from Horeb, in the second year, that he complained he could not bear the burden of government alone and established captains over thousands and hundreds and fifties and tens — which appears to be the very transaction recorded here, done on Jethro's advice. Moses speaks below of the statutes and laws of the Lord as things already revealed, which implies those laws had been given; and Jethro offers burnt-offerings apparently in the manner the law commands, though that law was not yet given. Clarke would therefore insert the chapter in Numbers, where Moses entreats Hobab to stay with them as a guide; but he adds that the matter is not of much importance. Ellicott meets the same difficulty more mildly, allowing that the mount of God may here be used broadly of the entire Sinaitic mountain region, or that the movement described in the next chapter may have taken place before Jethro's arrival though not related until after it, since Exodus was probably composed in detached portions and arranged afterwards.

Calvin is interested rather in what brought the old man out. It was not so much love for Moses as the fame of the miracles which drew him, bowed down with age, from his home into the wilderness; and that he was not induced by ambition will appear from the sequel, because after he had offered sacrifice to God and in solemn thanksgiving testified that he ascribed all the glory to God alone, he returned home again with the same simplicity in which he had come. Moses himself has already stated the cause at the head of the chapter, for he does not say Jethro had heard of the arrival of his son-in-law, but how wonderful had been God's goodness and power in delivering Moses and the people. He desired, therefore, to be in some measure a spectator of the things whereof he had heard, and not to neglect such illustrious instances of God's bounty by remaining at home. As to the title of the place, Calvin says the vision already vouchsafed there had made Horeb worthy of the name, but that the reference here is rather to the promulgation of the law, whereby God consecrated the mountain to Himself. Gill notices only that this is the third time in the chapter Jethro is called Moses's father-in-law, either to distinguish him or to do him honour.

Clarke offers one further reason why the account should stand where it does. Moses had just related the war with Amalek and the curse laid upon them, and may be supposed to have introduced the Midianite here to show Jethro free from that curse, although the Kenites of his family dwelt among the Amalekites. In consideration of Jethro, the Kenites who submitted to the Hebrews were suffered to live in their own country, though their land had been promised to the seed of Abraham. When Jethro speaks, the commentators agree he is not yet present. Gill takes it that he said it by a messenger, as Jarchi holds, or by a written letter, as Aben Ezra. Clarke concurs, since Moses goes out to meet him in the next verse, and supports it from the text, reading behold for I on the authority of the Greek and Syriac and several Samaritan copies, so that instead of I, thy father, we should read, Behold thy father.
7:
Henry makes the greeting a lesson in place. Though Moses was a prophet of the Lord, a great prophet, and king in Jeshurun, he showed a very humble respect to his father-in-law: however God in his providence is pleased to advance us, we must make conscience of giving honour to whom honour is due, and never look with disdain upon our poor relations. Those that stand high in the favour of God are not thereby discharged from the duty they owe to men, nor will that justify them in a stately haughty carriage. Moses went out to meet Jethro, did homage to him, and kissed him — religion does not destroy good manners. Even the kind enquiries after each other's welfare are taken notice of, Henry says, as the expressions and improvements of mutual love and friendship. Gill draws the same moral: one at the head of such a vast body of people condescended to go in person, when a guard of his men would have been honour sufficient. He adds, from Aben Ezra, that Moses is not said to go out to meet his wife and children, since it was not usual for honourable men so to do.

Ellicott sets the gestures among the customs of the country. Oriental etiquette required the going forth to meet an honoured guest, as with Abraham and Lot; the obeisance, however, was wholly voluntary, and marks the humility of Moses, who, now that he was the prince of his nation, might well have required Jethro to bow down to him. Kissing is a common form of salutation in the East, even between persons who are in no way related; Ellicott quotes Herodotus on the Persians, that when they meet each other in the streets you may know if the persons meeting are of equal rank by this token, for if they are, instead of speaking they kiss each other on the lips, while if one is a little inferior the kiss is given on the cheek. The asking after welfare he renders literally, that they wished peace to each other — the customary salutation, Peace be with you. Clarke reads the same three acts as good breeding and politeness accompanied with sincerity: bowing down the general token of respect, the kiss the token of friendship, the enquiry the proof of affectionate intercourse. On the tent they entered, Clarke reports that some understand the tabernacle, and that Moses may have taken his relative first to the house of God before bringing him to his own. Calvin notes only that the previous verse related what happened last, this transposition being common in Hebrew.

What follows the greeting Henry treats as a single movement. Conversation concerning God's wondrous works is profitable conversation, and asking and telling news is capable of being turned to good account by taking notice of God's providence in all occurrences. Jethro rejoiced not only in the honour done his son-in-law but in all the goodness done to Israel: public blessings are the joy of public spirits, and while the Israelites were themselves murmuring, here was a Midianite rejoicing — not the only time the faith of the Gentiles shamed the unbelief of the Jews. Whatever we have the joy of, God must have the praise of. His confession that the Lord is greater than all gods Henry takes as knowledge he had before but now held better, his faith grown to full assurance on this fresh evidence; its ground was that wherein the magicians and the idols and Pharaoh dealt proudly, God was above them. Sooner or later God will show himself above those who by their proud dealings contest with him. And Jethro, hearty in Israel's interests, was cheerfully admitted though a Midianite into fellowship with Moses and the elders, forasmuch as he also was a son of Abraham, though of a younger house.
8:
Calvin weighs the confession carefully and finds it genuine but not pure. It appears from it, he says, that although the worship of God was then everywhere profaned by strange additions, Jethro was not so devoted to superstition as to fail to honour the true God; and by the name Jehovah he plainly designates the God of Israel, confessing that the history of the deliverance had assured him of that God's immense power, so as to despise in comparison whatever gods were honoured elsewhere. Yet the comparison he adds, that Jehovah is greater than all gods, implies he was not free from all error. The prophets often speak so, but with a different import — sometimes exalting God above the angels, that His sole eminence may appear, sometimes calling Him greater not as if the false gods had any rank, but that the greatness falsely attributed to them may be brought to nothing. Jethro, however, imagines with the common notion that a multitude of inferior gods are subordinate to the Most High; and where the pure truth of God does not shine, religion is never clear, but always has some dregs mixed with it. Still Calvin allows him some advance, since in affirming that he now knows the power of God he implies he was more rightly informed than before — unless one prefers to understand it of the experimental knowledge which confirms even believers in a God they already knew. Clarke is firmer: some think Jethro was now converted, but he probably had this blessing before he knew anything of Moses, who would not likely have married into a heathen family.

The clause about dealing proudly divides them. Calvin observes that the sentence is unfinished — according to the word wherein they dealt proudly against them — the principal verb wanting to express that God repaid the Egyptians the just wages of their cruelty, as He denounces judgment without mercy on all who unmercifully mistreat their neighbours. The exposition some give, that the Egyptians who drowned the infants in the river were themselves drowned in the sea, seems to him too limited; he extends the clause to every punishment they received. Ellicott narrows it the other way, to the matter in which the Egyptians dealt most proudly — pursuing Israel with an army after giving them leave to depart, and attempting to recapture or destroy them. Clarke takes the pride to be their tyranny in enslaving God's people while purposing yet more, and God above them in showing himself superior to their gods by the miracles he wrought. Gill sees behind the idols the evil demons who influenced the magicians; Wesley reads the whole verse of princes as well as gods.

The sacrifice raises the question of Jethro's priesthood. Ellicott says he had brought the victims with him and now offered them in thankfulness for God's mercies to himself and his kinsman, occupying a position like Melchizedek's — a priesthood of the most primitive character, probably as patriarch of his tribe. As Abraham rightly acknowledged Melchizedek's priesthood, so Moses and Aaron acknowledged Jethro's, indicating their acceptance of it by sharing the sacrificial meal which followed. Calvin agrees that the meal proves the offering lawful, since the elders came not merely to eat bread with him but before God, an expression describing a solemn feast, and they would never have polluted themselves to gratify an unholy man; but he denies Jethro slew the victims in right of his Midianite priesthood, holding rather that there was more liberty before the law was given. By bread, Calvin adds, the manna is incontestably meant. Clarke, who has Jethro a priest by right, takes the burnt offering as presumptive evidence that the tabernacle was already erected, since before God means before the place where God dwelt; Wesley notes only that they ate soberly and thankfully, their talk such as became saints.
13:
Henry reads the day as a display of zeal. Having been employed to redeem Israel out of bondage, Moses is here a further type of Christ in being lawgiver and judge among them: his business was not to make laws but to make known God's, his place being that of a servant. Wesley says the same in a line, that he sat to answer enquiries and explain the laws already given; Clarke, that he heard and determined controversies, obliged to sit all day while the people were continually coming and going. Henry marks four things that might have excused him and did not. Though his father-in-law was with him, pretext enough for a vacation, he sat the next day from morning till evening — necessary business must take place of ceremonious attentions. Though advanced to great honour, he did not throw the burden of care upon others; those think of themselves above what is meet who think it below them to do good. Though the people had been ready to stone him, he still made himself the servant of all. And though an old man he kept to it from morning to night, proof that after all his labours his natural force was not diminished.

Calvin thinks the passage memorable because the fault is found in so good a man. In a government over which God presided, and which He honoured with extraordinary manifestations of His glory, there was something deserving reprehension; and Moses, with whom alone God was thus familiar, was deservedly reproved for wearing away both himself and the people by excessive labour. It was a magnanimity never sufficiently praised that he should occupy himself gratuitously for this perverse people though assailed by reproaches; yet Jethro finds occasion of fault in these very praises. Whence we are warned that in the most excellent acts of men some defect is ever lurking: let all, whether kings or magistrates or pastors, know that while they strain every nerve to fulfil their duties, something will always remain which may admit of correction. No single mortal can be sufficient to do everything — for who shall equal Moses, and he was unequal to the burden. Let God's servants learn to measure their powers, lest they wear out by ambitiously embracing too many occupations. As one ray of the sun does not illuminate the world but all combine as one, so God, that He may retain men in mutual society, unites one to another by variously dispensing His gifts, and raises up none out of measure by entire perfection. Calvin ends with Augustine, that God humbled His servant by this act, as Paul was buffeted lest his revelations exalt him.

Ellicott sets the scene in the institutions of the age. The office of prince or ruler was in early times regarded as including that of judge; rulers were sometimes even called judges, as were those of Israel from Joshua to Samuel, and ability to judge marked a person out as fit for the kingly office. Moses had from the first undertaken the hearing of all complaints, holding court days when the host was stationary; no cause was decided by anyone else, either because it had not occurred to him to discharge the duty by deputy, or because he thought his countrymen unfit. That the people stood by him all day shows the causes either very many or very hard; some have suggested that the division of the Amalekite spoil would have led to disputes. Keil adds that the people came to seek God, that is, to ask a decision from Him, and that by deciding the cases Moses made known the ordinances and laws of God — for every decision rested on some law, which, like all true justice, emanated first from God. Gill notes the Targum's dating of the morrow to the day after the atonement, preferring the day after Jethro came.
14:
The emphatic word in Jethro's question, Ellicott says, is alone: why dost thou not devolve a part of the duty upon others? Moses replies ingenuously, Calvin observes, like one unconscious of any fault, declaring himself the minister of God and the organ of His Spirit; his faithfulness could not be called in question, for he erred only in overwhelming himself with labour. Yet a useful lesson may be gathered from his words. He says that disputants come to inquire of God, and that he makes them know the statutes of God and His laws; hence it follows that this is the object of political government, that God's tribunal should be erected on earth, wherein He may exercise the judge's office — to the end that magistrates should not arrogate a power uncontrolled by any laws, nor assume what belongs to God. Then, and then only, will they acquit themselves properly: when they remember that they are the representatives of God. An obligation is here imposed upon private individuals also, that they should not rashly appeal to the authority of judges, but approach them with pure hearts, as if inquiring of God.

Gill, following Aben Ezra, distinguishes two things Moses did: teaching them the mind of God, and deciding causes where two persons could not agree. Clarke explains the first as mediation — Moses stood between God and the people, who came to him to know what God had spoken. Of the second Wesley remarks that if the people were as quarrelsome with one another as with God, he had many causes before him, the more because their trials put them to no expense. Clarke finds in the phrasing another argument for his chronology: the words about making them know the statutes of God are so particular that they leave little room for doubt the law had already been given.

Ellicott states Moses's two arguments more fully than Moses does. The people want decisions which they can feel to have divine sanction, and the ruling of inferior judges would not be regarded as equally authoritative; and Moses does not simply decide the question brought before him, but takes the opportunity to instruct the people in delivering his judgments, expounding principles and teaching morality. Both reasons, Ellicott says, were clearly of great weight and constituted strong arguments in favour of his practice — yet they failed to convince Jethro, who brought forward counter-arguments of his own. By continuing as hitherto Moses would exhaust both his own strength and the patience of the people; to keep suitors waiting all day and perhaps dismiss them untried was not fair upon them. Calvin admires the manner of the reproof. Jethro does not condemn the whole system Moses had adopted, after the fashion of morose or ambitious men who by carping at some trifle obscure the noble deeds of others; by correcting only a part he detracts nothing from the just praise of Moses, and leaves untouched the power God had conferred on him. Herein his moderation is worth observing, for he does not abuse the pretext of a particular error to upset the due order of things, but only advises Moses how he may usefully execute his office. Wesley compresses the verdict to a phrase: not good, that is, not convenient either for him or for them. On the warning itself Clarke renders the doubled Hebrew verb as in wearing away thou wilt wear away, so that Moses would soon become finally exhausted, and the people with him, since many wait so long that their patience must necessarily be worn out. Gill hears in the same word an allusion to the leaves of trees in autumn, which fade and wither and fall — Jethro feared constant attendance to business would impair a constitution naturally strong, though forty years later Moses's natural force was not abated.
19:
Clarke thinks Jethro a man of great understanding whose advice was probably given under the immediate inspiration of God, since after such sacrificial rites the prophetic spirit might well be expected to rest upon him. God could have shown Moses the necessity directly, but chose in this case to help man by man, and so laid a permanent basis for the union of the two families. Gill observes that Jethro, as the elder man and a prince of Midian, might counsel a younger man without censure. Ellicott renders the following clause as a wish — may God be with thee, may He give thee wisdom to direct the course aright — and reads the charge as an instruction to remain representative of the people towards God and of God towards the people, taking difficult causes to Him and expounding His laws. Calvin insists that Jethro does not rob Moses of his authority so as to overturn his call from God, but by exhorting him to proceed desires that what God has ordained should remain inviolable.

On the qualifications Calvin is fullest. The word rendered provide means to choose out and take the most worthy, so that such an office be not entrusted rashly to any that offers; and among a free people judges should be chosen not for wealth or rank but for superiority in virtue. Jethro enumerates four qualifications — ability in business, the fear of God, integrity, and contempt of riches — not to exclude the others named in Deuteronomy, but to signify that extraordinary virtues are wanted. The Hebrew men of might some take for strong and laborious men capable of bearing fatigue, but in Calvin's opinion Moses designates rather strenuous and courageous persons, opposed to the timid as well as the inactive. Because vigour of mind as well as body is frail without the fear of God, piety comes second, that they exercise their office as having an account to render; truth is opposed not only to gross falsehood but to popularity-hunting and flattery; and hatred of covetousness is demanded because nothing is more antagonistic to justice than eagerness for gain. Wesley puts it more briskly: clear heads and stout hearts make good judges. Ellicott notes that the last two requirements would approve themselves to men of all times and countries, while the first would generally be deemed superfluous, though it lies at the root of all excellence of character.

The organisation itself Ellicott finds unsurprising. In Egypt, as in all settled governments, the king was the fountain of justice but delegated the hearing of causes to officials of different ranks, and in Arabia a similar practice prevailed — Jethro himself had subordinates, the head men of the clans, who judged small matters. His advice was simply that Moses adopt this established system, on a decimal organisation which may already have existed for the march and the encamping: one man out of ten might judge small matters, with appeal to the ruler of fifty, then of a hundred, then of a thousand. Clarke traces the same ladder upward past Moses to God, and reports that some rabbins reckoned seventy-eight thousand six hundred officers in all; such computations, he says, are fanciful, since we cannot tell how many of each division there were. Ellicott adds that the judges were to sit not on occasional court days, as had been Moses's custom, but continually, and that it must have been left to them to decide what were great and what small matters. When the wilderness life ended, Jethro's system ended with it. Calvin reads the same impermanence in the text: Jethro had no wish to establish a law for posterity, but points out a provisional remedy, until the people should obtain a peaceful resting-place. He takes the clause about God commanding as a self-correction: Jethro would have nothing conceded to him which derogates from God's authority.
24:
Calvin finds the submission remarkable. Here is an instance of modesty, that Moses is not indisposed to submit to the counsel of his father-in-law; for although Jethro was his superior in age and affinity, in other respects he was far inferior to him. This yielding lays down a rule for all the greatest doctors, that they should not refuse the admonitions of those whom they admit to teach rightly, although they are not of such high dignity — for Cyprian truly declares that none is a good doctor who is not also docile. Wesley draws the same moral: those are not so wise as they would be thought to be who think themselves too wise to be counselled, for a wise man will hear and will increase learning, and not slight good counsel though given by an inferior. Gill says only that Moses weighed the advice well and judged it good, resolving to follow it when he had received directions from God.

Keil looks at the shape of the arrangement. The judges chosen were made chiefs over thousands, hundreds, fifties and tens, after the analogy of the military organisation on the march, but so that the arrangement was linked to the natural division of the people into tribes and families. That the decimal division was not made arbitrarily according to the number of heads is evident on two grounds: the judges were chosen from the heads of the tribes and according to their tribes; and the larger divisions of the tribes, the families, were themselves called thousands, because the number of their heads of families would generally average about a thousand. In all probability, then, the hundreds and fifties and tens denote smaller natural divisions rather than counted groups. Gill notices that though only the first of Jethro's qualifications is named in the record of the choice, no doubt all were attended to; and that the new judges sat any day in the week and any time in the day, whenever cases were brought before them.

The departure sets Clarke thinking about Moses himself. If this be the same transaction related in Numbers, it was with great reluctance that Moses let so able a counsellor go, pressing him to stay and be instead of eyes to them in the desert; but Jethro chose rather to return to his own country, where his family were probably too settled to be removed. Many others might be eyes to the Hebrews in the desert, but no man could be a father to his family but himself. It is well to labour for the public good, Clarke says, but our own families are the first claimants on our care and time. It is strange that after this we hear no more of Zipporah — forgotten merely because she was the wife of Moses, who chose to conduct himself so that to the remotest ages there should be proofs of his disinterestedness. While multitudes of the families of Israel are celebrated and dignified, his own he writes in the dust; he made no provision even for Gershom and Eliezer, whose families were incorporated with the Levites and had no higher employment than the care of the tabernacle. No history, Clarke concludes, has produced a parallel to this disinterestedness, and the one consideration is sufficient to refute every charge of imposture brought against him and his laws. Ellicott takes the dismissal as evidence against a common identification: the supposed identity of Hobab with Jethro seems precluded by it, for Hobab clearly remained till the close of the stay at Sinai, and Moses, instead of dismissing him, was most unwilling that he should depart. Gill reports the Targum's note that Jethro went to proselytise the children of his own country, and Wesley that the Kenites are supposed to be his posterity, taken afterwards under special protection for the kindness their ancestor showed Israel.
